title: Praise and blame
hookLine: favor and disgrace both unsettle us; care for the world as for your own body (Tao Te Ching 13)

lines: TWO MESSAGES FROM THE DINING ROOM.
COMPLIMENTS, AND A PLATE SENT BACK.
cards: A cook in a busy kitchen gets two messages from the dining room in the same minute. Table four sends compliments to the chef. Table nine sends a plate back.
One feels like sun, the other like a cold version.
An hour later, both are still replaying while the next orders wait, both pulling attention off the stove, both quietly handing the steering wheel to someone in the dining room.
Chapter thirteen of the Tao Te Ching puts praise and blame side by side and says something odd: they're the same kind of trouble.

teach.b: First, the claim. Favor and disgrace both startle a person, the chapter opens. Not just disgrace; favor too.
When you get favor, you're startled; when you lose it, you're startled again. Praise isn't a resting place. It's a thing you can now lose.
The chapter calls favor the lower thing, and readers take this more than one way. Some hear: to be favored is to stand beneath whoever does the favoring, so their approval becomes something you need.
Others hear simply that favor is worth less than people think. Either way, praise ties you to someone else's opinion as surely as blame does. Third, the body.
Then a startling question: why does a person have great troubles? Because they have a body, a self.

If there were no self, what trouble could reach them? Some readers hear this not as a call to give up the body, but as pointing at the part of a person that keeps score of how they're seen, where so much distress gathers.

teach.h: CARE FOR THE WORLD AS FOR YOUR BODY.
teach.b: Whoever values the whole world the way they value their own body, the chapter ends, can be trusted with the world.
The care you'd spend guarding your reputation, spend on everything else instead: from how am I seen, to what needs care.

how: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching use chapter thirteen as a check after praise or criticism: they notice how both pull at them, and turn their attention back to the work or the people in front of them.

o: the two sides of a court case in old China
favor and disgrace, both tied to others' opinion
a reward for good work and a fine for bad

p: comes from having a body, a self
who values it like their own body

s: chapter thirteen says praise is safe and only blame is a problem
favor and disgrace both startle: getting favor, and then losing it.
the chapter calls favor the lower thing
readers take it in more than one way, but it ties you to someone else's opinion.
the chapter tells people to stop caring about their bodies
some readers hear it pointing at the self that keeps score; the chapter turns that care outward to the world.

games.q: your boss praises your work in front of everyone. by chapter thirteen's light, what's the trouble with that?
o: none: praise is pure good news.
now there's something to lose, and it startles you both ways.
you should refuse to accept the praise.
games.why: favor startles when you get it and again when you lose it. the chapter doesn't say refuse it; it says notice the hook.

practice: Bring to mind a recent compliment and notice where it lands in the body: a warmth, a lift, a small wish to hear it again.

Don't push it away or hold on; let it pass like a car on the street outside, and if a criticism shows up instead, treat it the same way. Then let your attention turn to one person or one task that needs care.

wordCard.voice: Praise and blame. In chapter thirteen, favor and disgrace: two sides of one worry, both of them tied to someone else's opinion. Today's word.
